heading: What is OOPs & Why It Matters
subheading: The programming paradigm built around objects and real-world modeling
description:
Object-Oriented Programming (OOPs) is a programming paradigm that organizes software around objects — real-world-like entities that combine data (attributes) and behavior (methods) into a single unit.

**The four fundamental pillars of OOPs are:**
• **Encapsulation** — bundling data and methods together while controlling access.
• **Abstraction** — hiding internal complexity and exposing only what the user needs.
• **Inheritance** — creating new classes based on existing ones to reuse code.
• **Polymorphism** — allowing the same interface to behave differently depending on the context.

Why use OOPs?
• Makes large, complex software easier to design, understand, and maintain.
• Improves code reusability through inheritance and composition.
• Mirrors real-world relationships, making the code more intuitive.
• Widely adopted — Java, C++, Python, JavaScript, and PHP all support OOPs.

Note: Java is purely object-oriented (you cannot write a Java program without classes). C++ supports both OOP and procedural (C-style) programming.

heading: Class & Object
subheading: Blueprint vs instance — the foundation of everything in OOPs
description:
A class is a blueprint or template. It defines what data (fields) and behavior (methods) its objects will have, but it does not occupy memory by itself.

An object is a concrete instance of a class. When you create an object, memory is allocated on the heap to store its data, and it can then interact with other objects and the rest of the program.

Key points:
• A class is like an architectural plan; an object is the actual house built from it.
• You can create as many objects as you want from a single class.
• A class consumes no memory until an object is instantiated from it.
• An object of an empty class (no fields or methods) still occupies 1 byte in C++ — this is to give it a unique address in memory so that different objects can be distinguished.
• If a class has only static methods, you do not need to create an object — you can call those methods directly using the class name.

heading: Encapsulation
subheading: Wrapping data and methods together while protecting internal state
description:
Encapsulation is the process of bundling the data (fields) and the methods that operate on that data into a single unit — a class — while restricting direct access to the internal details.

It serves two purposes:
• **Data Hiding** — making fields private so external code cannot directly read or modify them. Access is provided through controlled getter and setter methods.
• **Data Binding** — keeping the data and the methods that manipulate it tightly coupled within the same class.

A fully encapsulated class has all its data members marked as private. This gives you complete control over how the data is accessed and modified, allows you to enforce validation rules, and makes the class easier to maintain.

Benefits:
• Protects object integrity by preventing invalid state changes.
• Improves code readability — all related logic lives in one place.
• Classes can be made read-only by providing only getters and no setters.

heading: Abstraction
subheading: Hiding complexity and showing only what the user needs to know
description:
Abstraction is about hiding the "how" and exposing the "what." As a user of a component, you should only need to know what it does, not how it works internally.

Think of a car — you know how to drive it (steering, accelerator, brake), but you do not need to understand how the engine, fuel injection system, and transmission work together under the hood. That complexity is abstracted away.

In programming, abstraction is achieved through:
• Abstract classes — classes with some implemented methods and some abstract (unimplemented) methods that subclasses must complete.
• Interfaces — contracts that define method signatures without any implementation.

Real examples of abstraction in practice: STL data structures like Stack and Queue. You use push(), pop(), enqueue(), and dequeue() without needing to know whether the underlying implementation uses an array or a linked list.

Abstraction vs Encapsulation:
• Abstraction hides the implementation details (what you see).
• Encapsulation hides the data and controls access (how it is protected).
Both work together — abstraction decides what to expose, and encapsulation enforces the boundary.

heading: Inheritance
subheading: Creating new classes by building on existing ones
description:
Inheritance allows a child class to acquire the properties and behaviors of a parent class, promoting code reuse and establishing a natural hierarchy between related classes.

Types of inheritance:
• **Single** — one child inherits from one parent.
• **Multiple** — one child inherits from two or more parents (supported in C++, not directly in Java).
• **Multi-level** — a chain where A → B → C (grandparent → parent → child).
• **Hierarchical** — multiple children inherit from the same parent.
• **Hybrid** — a combination of two or more types above.

Access rules when inheriting (C++ specific):
• Public inheritance — public stays public, protected stays protected, private is not inherited.
• Protected inheritance — public becomes protected, protected stays protected, private is not inherited.
• Private inheritance — everything becomes private (rarely used).

Limitations of inheritance:
• Tight coupling — changes in the parent class often require changes in all child classes.
• Increased complexity — deep inheritance chains are harder to understand and debug.
• Performance — navigating through multiple levels of inheritance adds processing overhead.

Prefer composition over inheritance when the relationship is "has-a" rather than "is-a."

heading: Polymorphism
subheading: One interface, many forms — decided at compile time or runtime
description:
Polymorphism means "many forms." It allows the same method name, operator, or interface to behave differently depending on the context.

Compile-time polymorphism (Static Polymorphism):
The compiler determines which version of a method or operator to use based on the arguments provided. This is resolved before the program runs.
• **Function Overloading** — multiple methods with the same name but different parameter lists.
• **Operator Overloading** — redefining what an operator (like +, -, ==) does for a custom class (supported in C++, not in Java).

Runtime polymorphism (Dynamic Polymorphism):
The decision about which method to call is made at runtime based on the actual type of the object, not the reference type. This is resolved during program execution.
• **Method Overriding** — a subclass provides its own implementation of a method defined in the parent class. The JVM uses the actual object type to decide which version to run.

Runtime polymorphism is what makes OOPs truly powerful — it allows you to write generic code that works with parent types but automatically calls the correct child implementation.

heading: Abstract Class vs Interface
description:
An abstract class is a class that cannot be instantiated directly. It can contain both fully implemented methods and abstract methods (methods with no body). Subclasses that inherit from it must provide implementations for all abstract methods, unless the subclass itself is also declared abstract.

An interface is a pure contract — traditionally, it contains only method signatures with no implementation at all. When a class implements an interface, it must provide the body for every method declared in the interface.

Key differences:
• Abstract class can have constructors, instance variables, and methods with any access modifier. Interface methods are public by default, and fields are public static final.
• A class can extend only one abstract class, but it can implement multiple interfaces.
• Abstract classes are used for sharing common code among closely related classes. Interfaces are used for defining capabilities that unrelated classes can share.

In Java 8+, interfaces can also have default methods (with a body) and static methods, blurring the line somewhat. However, the core distinction remains: abstract classes are about shared implementation, interfaces are about shared contracts.

heading: Diamond Problem & Multiple Inheritance
subheading: Why multiple class inheritance causes ambiguity and how languages solve it
description:
The Diamond Problem occurs in multiple inheritance when a class inherits from two classes that share a common ancestor. If both parent classes provide different implementations of the same method inherited from the common ancestor, the child class faces ambiguity — which version should it use?

The name comes from the diamond shape of the class hierarchy diagram: one grandparent at the top, two parents in the middle, and one child at the bottom.

How different languages handle it:
• Java avoids the problem entirely by not allowing multiple class inheritance. Instead, it uses interfaces. Since interfaces define contracts without implementation (and Java 8 default method conflicts must be explicitly resolved), there is no ambiguity.
• C++ allows multiple inheritance and solves the diamond problem using virtual inheritance (ensuring only one copy of the grandparent exists) or the scope resolution operator (::) to explicitly specify which parent's method to call.

heading: SOLID Principles
subheading: Five design principles for writing clean, maintainable, and scalable code
description:
**S — Single Responsibility Principle:**
A class should have only one reason to change. Each class should handle one specific job or responsibility. If a class is doing too many things, split it into smaller, focused classes.

**O — Open/Closed Principle:**
Classes should be open for extension but closed for modification. You should be able to add new behavior by extending a class (or implementing an interface), without changing the existing code that already works.

**L — Liskov Substitution Principle:**
A child class must be usable wherever its parent class is expected, without breaking the program. If replacing a parent object with a child object causes unexpected behavior, the inheritance hierarchy is poorly designed.

**I — Interface Segregation Principle:**
Do not force a class to implement methods it does not need. Instead of one large interface with many methods, create multiple smaller, focused interfaces. A class should only implement the interfaces that are relevant to it.

**D — Dependency Inversion Principle:**
High-level modules (business logic) should not depend directly on low-level modules (database, file system). Both should depend on abstractions (interfaces). This makes the system flexible — you can swap implementations without changing the high-level code.

heading: Constructors
subheading: Special methods that initialize objects when they are created
description:
A constructor is a special method that runs automatically when an object is created. Its name must match the class name, and it has no return type.

Types of constructors:
• **Default Constructor** — takes no arguments. If you do not define any constructor, the compiler provides one automatically that initializes fields to their default values.
• **Parameterized Constructor** — accepts arguments so you can set custom initial values when creating an object.
• **Copy Constructor** — creates a new object by copying the values from an existing object of the same class. In C++, this is built into the language. In Java, you implement it manually by writing a constructor that takes an object of the same class as a parameter.

Key points:
• Constructors cannot be inherited, but a child class can call the parent's constructor using super() (Java) or an initializer list (C++).
• If you define any parameterized constructor, the compiler no longer provides a default one — you must define it explicitly if you still need it.
• Constructors can be overloaded (multiple constructors with different parameter lists).

heading: Access Modifiers
subheading: Keywords that control who can see and use your classes, methods, and variables
description:
Access modifiers (also called access specifiers) determine the visibility and accessibility of classes, methods, and variables. They are essential for achieving encapsulation.

Four levels of access (from most restrictive to least):
• private — accessible only within the same class. No external class can see or use it.
• default (no keyword, package-private) — accessible within the same package only.
• protected — accessible within the same package and by subclasses in other packages.
• public — accessible from anywhere in the program.

Why they matter:
• They enforce encapsulation by hiding internal details and exposing only what is necessary.
• They prevent accidental misuse of internal methods or data.
• They make your code more secure and maintainable by defining clear boundaries between components.

In interfaces, methods are public by default, and fields are always public, static, and final.

heading: Static Keyword & this Pointer
subheading: Class-level members and self-referencing within an object
description:
The static keyword marks a member as belonging to the class itself, not to any particular object.
• A static variable is shared by all instances — there is only one copy in memory.
• A static method can be called using the class name without creating an object. It can only access other static members — it cannot use instance variables or the "this" pointer.
• A static function does not have a "this" reference because it is not tied to any specific object.

The "this" pointer (or "this" keyword in Java) is a reference to the current object — the object on which the method is being called. It is used to:
• Distinguish between instance variables and parameters when they share the same name.
• Pass the current object as an argument to another method.
• Call one constructor from another within the same class (constructor chaining).

heading: Destructors & Garbage Collection
subheading: How objects are cleaned up when they are no longer needed
description:
When an object is no longer needed, the memory it occupies must be freed to avoid memory leaks.

In C++, destructors handle this explicitly:
• For stack-allocated objects, the destructor is called automatically when the object goes out of scope.
• For heap-allocated objects (created with "new"), you must manually call "delete" to invoke the destructor and free the memory. Forgetting to do this causes memory leaks.

In Java, there are no destructors. Instead, Java uses Garbage Collection (GC) — an automatic process that identifies objects with no active references pointing to them and reclaims their memory.
• GC works only on heap memory.
• You cannot force it — System.gc() is just a suggestion.
• An object becomes eligible for GC when all references to it are removed, set to null, or go out of scope.

The key takeaway: C++ gives you manual control (and responsibility) over memory. Java handles it automatically through GC, trading some performance for safety and convenience.

heading: Exception Handling
subheading: Catching and managing errors gracefully so your program does not crash
description:
An exception is an unexpected event that occurs during program execution and disrupts the normal flow — for example, dividing by zero, accessing a null reference, or reading a file that does not exist.

Exception handling is the mechanism for anticipating these situations, catching them, and defining how the program should respond instead of crashing.

The standard approach uses try-catch-finally:
• try — wraps the code that might throw an exception.
• catch — defines what to do when a specific exception occurs.
• finally — runs cleanup code regardless of whether an exception was thrown (e.g., closing files or database connections).

Other constructs:
• throw — explicitly raise an exception from your code.
• throws (Java) — declare in a method signature that it might throw certain exceptions.

Why it matters: no one wants their software to crash in front of users. Exception handling lets you deal with errors gracefully, log them for debugging, and keep the program running. It separates the error-handling logic from the main business logic, making both easier to read and maintain.

heading: Class vs Structure
subheading: How classes and structs differ in memory, access, and purpose
description:
Although classes and structures look similar, they serve different purposes and behave differently in key ways.

Memory allocation:
• Structures are typically stored on the stack (value types), making them faster to allocate and deallocate.
• Classes are stored on the heap (reference types), with references to them kept on the stack.

Default access:
• In C++, struct members are public by default, while class members are private by default.
• In Java, there are no structs — everything is a class.

Capabilities:
• Classes support all OOPs features: inheritance, polymorphism, abstraction, and encapsulation.
• Structures in C++ can also have methods and inheritance, but they are traditionally used for simple data grouping without complex behavior.

When to use which:
• Use a struct for lightweight data containers with little or no behavior (e.g., a Point with x and y coordinates).
• Use a class when you need encapsulation, inheritance, polymorphism, or complex logic.
